newsitem.title: USA: Wall St stocks seen opening higher, data due.
newsitem.headline: Wall St stocks seen opening higher, data due.

text.p: Wall Street stocks were expected to open stronger Friday, with spill-over momentum from furious buying late yesterday fueling the Dow.
Yesterday the Dow Industrials roared back from whopping losses, with late computer buying programs helping the index close nearly unchanged.
"We should open on a firm note, carrying forward the momentum from yesterday," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst for Prudential Securities.

The Dow Industrials closed off six points at about 6442 Thursday. The index fell over 90 points at its nadir after a big rise in manufacturing activity startled the bond market and sent yields soaring.
Markets are anxiously awaiting the release of November U.S. construction spending, due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT. Spending is forecast to fall 0.6 percent, compared to a rise of 1.8 percent in October.
"I don't expect it to be major, but anything can happen" if the forecasts are way off, Wachtel said.

The dollar extended gains against the mark, trading about a pfennig up from Thursday's close. Against the yen, the greenback was steady and firm in thin trading, awaiting the construction spending figures.
Financial markets in Tokyo remained closed for the New Year holiday.
Hong Kong stocks closed higher with volume heavy.
The Hang Seng blue-chip index held steady above the key 13,200 level, closing 19.35 points higher at 13,222.8 after seesawing within a 100-point band.
London stocks were higher, with the FTSE 100 index up 24 points to 4081, recovering nearly a third of its losses yesterday.
U.S. shares traded in London were mostly higher, but trading volume was still light. Automakers Chrysler Corp and Ford Motor Co showed slight strength.
Certain technology shares, which were roundly battered in New York yesterday, rebounded slightly in London, including Compaq Computer Corp and Dell Computer Corp.
A pall has been cast over the retail industry, the Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column said, and investors are selling retail stocks because of fears about weak holiday sales.

Liberty Media Corp Chairman John Malone wants to gain more control of the cable programming company by taking over the stake left by the late Bob Magness, according to the New York Times Marketplace column.
